extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, attorneys, and legal professionals involved in USPTO/OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used by the USPTO (OED) and courts to establish professional misconduct by patent practitioners and to determine appropriate sanctions. Covers elements of specific rule violations, summary-judgment proof requirements, and aggravating/mitigating factors for sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to establish violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish Respondent’s liability for violating 37 C.F.R. § 11.304(c), the OED Director must show that Respondent is: (1) a practitioner who (2) had an obligation under the rules of a tribunal (3) that he disobeyed (4) knowingly, and (5) he did not make an open refusal based on an assertion that no valid obligation exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term “tribunal” is defined in the PTO Rules as including a court (37 C.F.R. § 11.1). “Knowingly” is defined as actual knowledge of the fact in question and may be inferred from circumstances. The Model Rule 3.4(c) (ABA) is virtually the same and its interpretations and state disciplinary opinions can be instructive in construing the PTO rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: failure to pay court-ordered sanction may violate § 11.304(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to pay a court-ordered sanction can constitute disobeying 'an obligation under the rules of a tribunal' within the meaning of § 11.304(c) where the practitioner disregarded a tribunal ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a strict textual read might limit § 11.304(c) to rules of procedure/evidence, precedent applying Model Rule 3.4(c) to failures to comply with court orders (including financial obligations like child support or court costs) supports application. Cases cited: People v. Sanders; Braswell; In re Williams; Florida Bar v. Committe; People v. Quigley. Particular relevance when sanction concerns client restitution or malpractice related to patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d): conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to comply with court-ordered financial obligations, failure to comply with discovery, failure to respond to motions, or other conduct that results in actual prejudice to the court can constitute such misconduct. Case examples include Sanders, Wiles, and others. Failure to respond to the PTO's requests that hampers its investigation has been treated similarly (Bender).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i): 'other conduct' must be distinct from (a)-(h)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.804(i) prohibits 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner’s fitness to practice before the Office,' but conduct cannot be found to violate § 11.804(i) if it is prohibited by § 11.804(a)–(h).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Moatz v. Colitz (and Review Dept. precedent), to qualify as 'other' conduct under the analogous Code provision, the conduct must be outside the scope of the enumerated prohibitions. Thus do not duplicate findings under (i) and another subsection for the same facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b): failure to cooperate / knowingly failing to respond to an RFI
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not fail to disclose a fact necessary to correct a misapprehension, fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation, or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from a disciplinary authority (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish violation, OED must show either failure to cooperate in an investigation or that the practitioner knowingly failed to respond to an RFI lawfully issued pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f)(1)(ii). Proof points: that the RFI was lawfully issued, practitioner received it, and practitioner did not respond or request an extension. Follow-up 'Lack of Response' notices and receipt of those letters strengthen OED's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary-judgment proof requirements in disciplinary proceedings (FRCP 56 standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: To defeat summary judgment a party must raise a genuine dispute of material fact supported by 'citing to particular materials in the record' (depositions, documents, affidavits, admissions, etc.) per FRCP 56(c)(1)(A), and produce sufficient evidence that a jury could return a verdict in its favor (Liberty Lobby/477 U.S. standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsupported assertions or conclusory defenses in an answer may be deemed abandoned or insufficient if not supported by record citations. Failure to cite evidence or to explain why an extension could not have been requested undermines impossibility defenses. Courts regularly deem unproffered affirmative defenses abandoned at summary judgment (Mattolo; Pittston).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility challenges insufficient to defeat summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad, conclusory attacks on witness credibility will not, by themselves, present questions of material fact sufficient to defeat summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party 'cannot defeat summary judgment merely by impugning a [witness'] honesty'—must provide admissible evidence creating a genuine issue (Island Software; McCullough).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comity and res judicata limits in disciplinary context
rubrics_metrics.description: Res judicata bars relitigation of a claim only where a court has rendered a final judgment on the merits of the same claim or cause of action; comity involves reciprocal recognition of sister-jurisdiction disciplinary acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a state proceeding or final judgment, OED may still discipline a practitioner. The absence of state bar action means there is no judicial act to trigger comity in favor of declining sanction. Kroll supports Director's broad authority to discipline even when states have not acted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility / inability-to-pay defense requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions of inability to pay a court-ordered sanction must be timely raised, supported by evidence, and/or relief sought in the original court; mere assertion in an answer without record support is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities indicate inability to pay is not a defense where the attorney knew of the order but took no steps to seek relief in the issuing court (Florida Bar v. Committe; In re Respondent Y). Failure to present evidence at summary judgment means the defense may be deemed abandoned (Mattolo; Pittston; FRCP 56).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining sanctions the PTO Rules require consideration of: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of disciplinary rules is remedial—not punitive—and aims to protect the public, preserve integrity of the profession, and deter misconduct. The central issue is whether the accused is a 'fit and proper person' to continue practicing. The PTO has used ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors (ABA Standards § 9.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors to consider in sanctioning include: (a) prior disciplinary offenses; (b) dishonest or selfish motive; (c) a pattern of misconduct; (d) multiple offenses; (e) bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding by intentionally failing to comply with rules or orders; (f) submission of false evidence/false statements/deceptive practices during the process; (g) refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct; (h) vulnerability of victim; (i) substantial experience in the practice of law; (j) indifference to making restitution; (k) illegal conduct, including controlled-substance involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED and courts commonly apply these factors; several were applied by the OED Director as justification for exclusion (prior discipline, dishonest motive, pattern, obstruction, lack of remorse, substantial experience, indifference to restitution). Aggravating factors support harsher sanctions including exclusion/disbarment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors (ABA Standards § 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors include: (a) absence of a prior disciplinary record; (b) absence of dishonest or selfish motive; (c) personal or emotional problems; (d) timely good-faith effort to make restitution or rectify consequences; (e) full and free disclosure to disciplinary board or cooperative attitude; (f) inexperience in practice; (g) character or reputation; (h) physical disability; (i) mental disability or chemical dependency; (j) delay in disciplinary proceedings; (k) imposition of other penalties or sanctions; (l) remorse; (m) remoteness of prior offenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigating factors, when proven, can reduce severity of sanction. The absence of any mitigating evidence (e.g., no remorse, no restitution efforts) supports imposition of more severe discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction proportionality and multiple offenses guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple charges exist the sanction should be at least consistent with the sanction for the most serious instance of misconduct, and generally greater when there is a pattern or multiple instances of misconduct (ABA Standards, Theoretical Framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should reflect the aggregate seriousness; pattern or multiple offenses are aggravating and justify greater discipline (e.g., exclusion versus suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: OED proof approach for RFI/nonresponse cases
rubrics_metrics.description: OED establishes liability for non-cooperation by proving lawful issuance of an RFI, practitioner’s receipt of the RFI and follow-up notices, and practitioner's failure to respond or to request an extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary proof of mailing/receipt and records of lack of response, together with admissions by practitioner of receipt, are dispositive. Courts have treated repeated failure to respond to lawful demands as conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (Bender; Bromwell).
